reading.title: Practice Round
reading.purpose: Listen in as a debate coach helps a student turn an opinion into an argument.
paras: "Read me your first claim again," Coach Reyes said, leaning on the desk. Imani checked her notes. "My stance is that our town should turn the empty lot on Pine Street into a community garden. I contend that it would do more good than a parking lot." Coach Reyes nodded. "Good. Now convince me."

Imani listed her reasons. "My first premise is that the lot has sat empty for six years. My second premise is that families nearby have no place to grow food. So a garden would put unused land to work." Coach Reyes tapped the page. "I like the logic, since each step leads to the next. But I still need a warrant, the reason that connects your evidence to your claim. Why does it matter that the land would be used?" Imani thought for a moment. "Because land that neighbors use stays cleaner and safer than land nobody watches."

"Now argue against yourself," the coach said. "Give me a counterclaim." Imani winced. "Someone will say we need the parking, because shoppers have to park somewhere." "Then make a concession," Coach Reyes said. "Admit what is fair in it. After that, rebut it." Imani began again. "I agree that parking matters. But the street already has forty spaces, and a half-empty lot does not solve a problem that is not there."

"Careful," the coach warned. If Imani said that people who want parking do not care about food, she would be using a fallacy. Coach Reyes explained that a fallacy is a mistake in reasoning, such as attacking the people instead of answering their point. Imani crossed out the line. "What can I add to substantiate my claim?" she asked. "Evidence," said Coach Reyes. "Count the cars that actually park there on a Saturday. Ask twenty neighbors what they would plant."

Imani spent the weekend collecting numbers. On Monday she read her argument aloud again, and this time every part had a place. When she finished, Coach Reyes smiled. "That is what a real argument looks like. Not louder, just stronger."

qs.q: In paragraph 2, the word "warrant" most nearly means
choices: an official paper that gives someone the right to enter a place
a list of facts that a speaker has gathered from many sources
a promise that a claim will turn out to be true in the end
a reason that connects evidence to a claim
qs.why: Coach Reyes defines it in the same sentence: a warrant is "the reason that connects your evidence to your claim."

qs.q: Which sentence explains what a fallacy is?
choices: Coach Reyes explained that a fallacy is a mistake in reasoning, such as attacking the people instead of answering their point.
If Imani said that people who want parking do not care about food, she would be using a fallacy.
Ask twenty neighbors what they would plant.
qs.why: This sentence gives the meaning directly: a mistake in reasoning, such as attacking people rather than answering their point.

ev.text: Coach Reyes explained that a fallacy is a mistake in reasoning, such as attacking the people instead of answering their point.

qs.q: Why does Coach Reyes ask Imani to argue against herself?
choices: so that she can replace her own claim with the opposite one before Monday
so that she can prepare answers to the points other people will raise
so that she can learn whether the coach agrees with her stance
so that she can prove to the audience that her side has no weak spots
qs.why: Imani names a counterclaim and then answers it with a concession and a rebuttal, which prepares her for the objections she will hear.

qs.q: Which statement best sums up what Imani learns?
choices: A strong argument is simply louder and much longer than the argument on the other side.
An argument is finished as soon as a speaker has stated a clear opinion.
A strong argument ties reasons to evidence and answers the other side fairly.
A speaker should avoid mentioning the points that other people might make.
qs.why: Throughout the practice round, the coach asks for a warrant, a fair answer to the other side, and evidence, and ends by saying "stronger," not louder.

clues.text: the reason that connects your evidence to your claim
Admit what is fair in it.
a mistake in reasoning, such as attacking the people instead of answering their point
